summary: Fine-tuning makes sense when you need to change a model's behavior, tone, or output format consistently, or when you need to encode specialized domain knowledge and patterns that prompting alone can't reliably achieve. Use RAG when the task requires access to frequently-changing or proprietary factual data, and use prompt engineering first for most tasks since it is the cheapest and fastest to iterate on. Fine-tuning shines after you've exhausted prompting and RAG, have hundreds to thousands of high-quality labeled examples, and need lower latency or cost at scale.
when_to_fine_tune: Choose fine-tuning when you need consistent output structure, tone, or style that few-shot prompting fails to reliably enforce across inputs.
Choose fine-tuning for domain adaptation or instruction tuning when you have hundreds to thousands of high-quality labeled examples that capture the desired behavior.
Prefer RAG over fine-tuning when the knowledge is factual, frequently updated, or must be cited, since fine-tuning bakes in static knowledge that is costly to refresh.
Fine-tune to reduce inference cost and latency at scale by shrinking long prompts into learned behavior, especially when deploying smaller open-source models in production.
